title: MagnaCut Folding Knife
coverAlt: Finished folding knife with its steel blade open and wooden handle visible
summary: Designed and fabricated a folding knife with a CPM MagnaCut blade that averaged 63 HRC across three tests.
lede: Our team designed and fabricated a back-lock folding knife for camping use. We chose CPM MagnaCut and selected a heat treatment intended to balance blade hardness with toughness.
sections: Mechanism and fabrication

We modeled the knife in SolidWorks in both open and closed positions, then fabricated the blade and assembled the folding mechanism. We built a dedicated bevel jig to hold the blade during grinding on the belt sander.
Heat treatment and verification

We planned the heat treatment with a thermal history plot and used stainless tool wrap to limit oxidation and decarburization during hardening. The sequence included quenching, cold treatment, and two tempering cycles. After processing, three Rockwell C measurements averaged 63 HRC, within the team’s target range.

title: Manifold / Thruster Study
coverAlt: Simulated Mach number contour through a converging-diverging nozzle
summary: Studying how to distribute regulated nitrogen to a spacecraft’s cold gas thrusters, alongside the propulsion team’s nozzle trade study.
lede: Our propulsion team is studying a nitrogen cold gas system for spacecraft attitude adjustments. I work on the manifold that distributes regulated gas to the thruster branches.
sections: Manifold design

I’m comparing off-the-shelf and custom manifolds, with attention to pressure ratings and how much flow each branch needs when multiple valves open. One trade is whether to use a pressure relief device downstream of the regulator or rate the downstream components for exposure to full storage pressure. The final architecture and verification plan are still in development.
Nozzle sizing trade study

The propulsion team varied the exit-to-throat area ratio across several thrust targets using a modeled 20 bar nitrogen inlet and vacuum exhaust. Increasing the ratio improved predicted specific impulse, with diminishing gains as the nozzle grew wider and longer. Comparing a conical profile with a shorter bell profile helped put those efficiency gains in the context of available space.
What the simulation shows

The team used SolidWorks Flow Simulation on a conical nozzle candidate labeled for a 75 mN design target. The model applied mass flow at the inlet and an environment pressure condition at the exit. The Mach contour predicts acceleration through the throat and supersonic flow downstream. This is a team simulation; the design target is not a measured thrust result.

title: L1 Rocket
coverAlt: Completed red and black L1 rocket with conical nose and laser-cut fins
summary: Designed and fabricated flight hardware, modeled stability in OpenRocket, and documented the launch.
lede: I designed and 3D printed the conical nose cone, laser cut the fins, and 3D printed the motor retainer. I used OpenRocket to compare motor configurations and evaluate stability before launch.
facts: Printed nose cone and laser-cut fins
sections: From CAD to airframe

The final nose cone used a straight conical profile with a shoulder to locate it in the body tube. I translated the fin profile into laser-cut parts and used a printed motor retainer to secure the motor in the airframe.
Stability and simulation

I compared H-class motor configurations and checked the location of the center of pressure relative to the center of gravity. The static margin expresses that separation in body diameters, or calibers. The figures above are from the H219T-14 simulation and are not measured flight data.

title: Tethered Weather Balloon
coverAlt: Breadboard and sensor wiring assembled inside a black louvered balloon payload enclosure
summary: Designed a sensor payload to study air quality at different heights above Mt. SAC, with onboard logging and a LoRa link.
lede: I led a team building a tethered balloon payload to profile how air quality changes with height above Mt. San Antonio College in Walnut, California. The project combined mechanical packaging, embedded electronics, and ground operations.
sections: Payload enclosure

We chose ASA for outdoor UV and temperature exposure. The enclosure made room for the sensor breadboard, with a louvered panel and a dedicated opening for the LoRa antenna. We estimated balloon lift from payload mass and used the expected loads to evaluate the eye bolt and select a tether within our length and budget limits. A manual winch was planned for recovery.
Sensing and logging

I drew the KiCad schematic for the Pico, Pi Zero 2 W, radio, camera, and sensor connections. The breadboard integrated the BME280, MiCS-6814, MQ-131, and PMS5003 for atmospheric and air quality measurements. Python and MicroPython handled sensor acquisition; the Pi logged readings to a CSV on its SD card. LoRa was intended to send a second copy to the ground if the payload could not be recovered.
Field outcome

The balloon burst during inflation after contact with a hot metal bar, so the payload never flew and we collected no altitude profile. A loose camera ribbon also prevented planned footage. For a repeat attempt, I would isolate the balloon from hot surfaces, secure the camera connector, and verify recording and telemetry on flight power before inflation.

title: L2 Rocket
coverAlt: OpenRocket side profile of the L2 rocket showing nose, body tubes, and fins
summary: Developing a four-inch high-power airframe with dual deployment and space for onboard instrumentation.
lede: I’m designing and building a rocket for Level 2 certification. The project extends my L1 build into recovery electronics, airframe integration, and onboard instrumentation.
sections: Airframe layout

I’m using OpenRocket to evaluate component placement, center of gravity, and center of pressure. The current layout defines the nose cone, body tubes, couplers, bulkheads, and fin sets. The layout view shows the airframe without a selected motor.
Recovery and instrumentation

The recovery layout uses a drogue in the lower section and a main parachute under the nose, with an electronics bay for deployment control. I’m also planning a compact payload bay for a camera and an accelerometer/gyroscope to examine flight events.

title: Tensile Testing and Hardness
coverAlt: Rows of polymer and metal specimens showing fractures from tensile testing
summary: Compared filleted and square-shouldered specimens across four materials and examined how they deformed and fractured.
lede: Our lab team compared the tensile response of PLA, aluminum, galvanized steel, and MagnaCut. Testing both filleted and square-shouldered specimens let us observe the influence of geometry alongside differences between materials.
sections: Tensile response

We compared measured stress–strain curves and inspected the specimens after testing for necking and fracture location. The results showed why geometry matters when interpreting a tensile test: a break near a shoulder may tell you as much about the local stress concentration as about the material itself.
Hardness comparison

We also took Rockwell readings on forged, control, and drilled metal coupons. The original lab sheet records the readings and scales. I would verify the scale and repeatability before treating any of those values as a material property.

title: METAL Level 1 Manufacturing Workshop
coverAlt: Haas Mini Mill CNC machining the cast aluminum truck to remove excess material and surface imperfections
summary: Hands-on aluminum casting, lathe work, CNC milling, and steel heat treatment, with a focus on designing for manufacturability.
lede: At Cal Poly Pomona’s METAL Level 1 workshop, I made aluminum parts using green sand and lost foam casting, then practiced lathe work, CNC milling, and steel heat treatment. Taking designs from CAD through casting and finishing helped me understand manufacturing processes and the importance of designing for manufacturability.
facts: Casting, lathe work, and CNC milling
sections: Green sand casting and machining

We poured molten aluminum into a green sand mold to create the truck body, turned its wheels on a lathe, and CNC milled the casting on a Haas Mini Mill to remove excess material and surface imperfections. Working through casting and machining showed me how the initial shape and finishing operations work together to produce the completed part.
Lost foam casting

We modeled the horse in CAD and made foam patterns from the design. The patterns were packed in sand and replaced by molten aluminum during pouring to form the horse casting. I also used Fusion 360 for modeling and FLOW-3D CAST to look for potential shrinkage defects.
Designing for manufacturability

Making both aluminum castings helped me connect design decisions to the manufacturing process. I learned to consider how a shape will be cast, which surfaces will need machining, and how the part can be held and reached by the tools. The experience reinforced the importance of planning fabrication and finishing while developing the design.
Heat treatment trade-offs

We used time–temperature–transformation diagrams to reason about how thermal history changes steel microstructure. We then secured heat-treated coupons in a vise to compare their behavior. The exercise made the trade-off tangible: hardness helps resist indentation and wear, while ductility and toughness matter when a part must deform or absorb energy before fracturing.
